column3: It repeats the verdict that their claim lacks knowledge and rests only on conjecture, applied to an account of life and death.
It directly rebukes the same unequal assignment of daughters to God and sons to people that frames the focus's angel claim.
It opposes human religious claims to God's comprehensive knowledge, reinforcing the focus's denial that the speakers know divine intent.
It closely repeats the fatalistic excuse, then answers it with the lack of knowledge and reliance on conjecture.
It begins the local critique of assigning a share of God's servants to Him, the premise developed into the focus's worship claim.
It states divine willing without turning that fact into an authorization for a human act, clarifying the focus's false inference.
It gives the near-verbatim claim that God's will would have prevented their worship, then redirects to the messengers' clear delivery.
The immediately preceding verse calls their angel classification unsupported testimony, supplying the claim the focus then rationalizes.
God's comprehensive knowledge governs inheritance priorities here, without a claim about divine will, worship, or conjecture.
The deniers reject a message from the Merciful as a lie, broadly paralleling the focus's false speech about Him.
It challenges the same daughter-for-God and son-for-them division underlying the claim about female angels.
Its condemnation of the conjecturers directly names the epistemic fault identified at the end of the focus.
It links following conjecture with fabricating estimates and being led from God's way, expanding the focus's final diagnosis.
It immediately exposes the inconsistency of attributing daughters to God while reserving sons for themselves.
The impotence of invoked beings to create does not address the focus's inference from divine willing to worship permission.
It describes associators as following only conjecture and estimating falsely, closely matching the focus's criticism of their worship claim.
The next local response replaces evidence with inherited custom, showing how the focus's unsupported claim becomes a claimed path of guidance.
It qualifies human certainty about a future act by God's will, but does not treat that will as a defense of worship.
Its demand to identify a guarantor exposes an unsupported assertion, a concise parallel to the focus's challenge to their alleged knowledge.
It shows people returning to association after relief, a behavioral parallel to attributing worship to God's will without evidence.
Divine witness over all things is not connected here to a speculative claim or to worship authorization.
It explicitly describes worship beside God as lacking both revealed authority and knowledge, directly supporting the focus's epistemic rebuke.
It continues the local account of their gendered valuation that makes the assignment of female angels rhetorically inconsistent.
The garden's undiminished yield belongs to its narrative and does not clarify the focus's claim about will or knowledge.
It states the claim that the Merciful has taken a child, a close theological parallel to the false attributions surrounding the focus.
Its coming questioning gives the local speech an accountability horizon, but does not itself address the false causal inference.
It links understanding to knowledge, offering a general contrast to the focus's declaration that its speakers lack knowledge.
It restates the claim that the Merciful has taken a child and corrects it by calling the angels honored servants.
The assurance that no deed is lost does not bear on the focus's worship claim or its epistemic critique.
God's knowledge of what is hidden and disclosed generally contrasts with the speakers' lack of knowledge of His will.
Its rejecters use divine will to dismiss the summons to worship God alone, closely paralleling the focus's causal excuse.
This local objection concerns the social status of a messenger rather than the focus's claim about divine will and worship.
The warning that most wrongdoers do not know does not identify a comparable inference or act of worship.
Calling the message clear magic is another denial, but its link to conjecture or the will-based excuse is indirect.
It presses the question whether they witnessed the creation of female angels, directly challenging the claim developed in the focus.
The question about human creation from a thing does not materially connect to speculative worship claims.
It affirms God's power to make one community while preserving His mercy and judgment, a corrective context for simplistic appeals to divine will.
Jesus' clarification of disputed matters does not address the focus's claim about worship or unsupported knowledge.
Divine testimony and knowledge validate revelation, generally contrasting with the focus's speakers who claim knowledge without warrant.
The Merciful's knowledge of the unseen and seen is a broad contrast to human guessing about His intention.
The creation of male and female does not itself address the false assignment of gender to angels or worship.
God's knowledge of concealed and public speech broadly answers the focus's false utterance, without repeating its causal logic.
The promise of affection for believers is unrelated to worship excused through divine willing.
Moses' mission to Pharaoh does not materially clarify the focus's speculative claim.
Mocking a known sign illustrates rejection after evidence, though not the particular inference from God's will to worship permission.
It contrasts outward speech with concealed reality known to God, sharpening the focus's exposure of a claim made without knowledge.
It directly condemns assigning daughters to God while keeping what they desire for themselves, the same asymmetry behind the angel claim.
Ignorance of revealed boundaries among desert Arabs is not a close parallel to the focus's stated conjecture.
Its deniers defend ancestral worship and dismiss revelation as fabrication, a related pattern of preserving worship through false speech.
The local speakers use contentious comparison rather than evidence, paralleling the focus's speculative argumentative posture.
The sleepers defer disputed duration to God's knowledge, providing a limited positive contrast to asserting what one does not know.
It makes choosing a path to God contingent on willing, but does not license a wrongful act by that condition.
Their distress at news of a daughter exposes the social valuation that makes their attribution of daughters to God incoherent.
The statement that whoever wills may remember has no material link to their excuse for worship.
God's mercy and restraint amid unrecognized believers concern a distinct situation, not a conjectural claim about worship.
The local lament over a people who do not believe continues the surrounding rejection context without restating the focus's inference.
Divine favor and knowledge here do not address worship, conjecture, or a claim about God's will.
It declares that neither they nor their fathers have knowledge of their claim and calls their speech a lie.
It requires evidence for an alleged divine prohibition and rejects following desire, closely paralleling the focus's unsupported attribution of intent.
It limits the opponents' knowledge and contrasts it with God's knowledge of the guided and astray, supporting the focus's epistemic judgment.
It explicitly says they have no knowledge, follow only conjecture, and that conjecture cannot replace truth.
It directly addresses the claim about a child for the Merciful through a conditional formulation, continuing the local correction of false attributions.
The future knowledge warning does not identify the present false inference or worship claim.
Their refusal of the declaration of God's oneness supplies the monotheistic opposite of the worship defended in the focus.
It affirms God's conclusive proof while distinguishing His will from the opponents' unsupported claims about guidance.
Divine clarification before judgment is a general principle, without a matching claim of conjectural worship.
The angels acknowledge that they know only what God taught, a modest contrast to speakers claiming knowledge of His will.
The local promise that they will know completes the rebuke, but adds no specific account of the false causal inference.
A soul's knowledge of what it brought concerns final accounting rather than the focus's claim about divine willing.
The demand for a sign is answered by God's power and their lack of knowledge, but not by an excuse for worship.
The reference to a emitted drop has no material link to the focus's worship or conjecture.
The repeated warning that they will know is too general to clarify the focus's specific claim.
It clearly dissociates the speaker from the opponents' worship, supplying a direct monotheistic contrast to the focus's defended practice.
Abraham's disavowal of what his people worship directly opposes the worship the focus's speakers seek to justify.
The warning that distracted deniers will know does not illuminate the focus's argument from divine will.
Mocking the messenger who mentions their gods reflects resistance to monotheism, but without the focus's epistemic formula.
God's measured knowledge of gestation is unrelated to worship excused by His will.
God's knowledge of the unseen and of deeds generally contrasts with speculation about His intention.
The divine name alone provides no substantive connection to the focus's claim.
Pharaoh's people promise guidance in return for relief, but do not make the focus's will-based claim about worship.
The future knowledge warning remains too general to establish a material link.
It closely repeats the excuse that, if God had willed, He would have acted Himself, using it to refuse a commanded duty.
It demands knowledge for alleged divine prohibitions, directly challenging the kind of unsupported attribution to God made in the focus.
The dispute over payment for repairing a wall does not bear on worship, conjecture, or divine will.
The name Merciful and Compassionate alone does not provide a material connection.
It rejects inherited guidance even when a better path is brought, directly continuing the local refusal that follows the focus.
Its creation signs address doubt about resurrection, not an unsupported claim that worship was divinely authorized.
It combines lack of knowledge with following conjecture in a disputed historical claim, closely matching the focus's epistemic formula.
Human origin, diversity, and piety do not materially clarify the focus's false claim about divine will.
It describes people as especially contentious despite varied examples, broadly resembling the argumentative resistance in the focus.
It rebukes an ignorant conjecture about God and corrects a fatalistic counterfactual, closely paralleling the focus's reasoning.
Divine favor and wisdom here are not tied to worship, conjecture, or a claimed intent.
God's knowledge of devotional circumstances and resulting ease do not address the focus's causal excuse.
The Creator's intimate knowledge broadly contradicts attempts to infer His hidden intention without knowledge.
The command to follow revelation and turn from associators supplies only broad background, without the focus's specific logic.
It states God's exclusive power to bring or remove harm and grant favor, framing divine willing without treating it as worship authorization.
The sudden appearance at resurrection does not address the focus's claim.
The Quran's universal reminder is not a material parallel to the will-based excuse or conjecture.
The separation of hypocrites and believers at judgment does not clarify the focus's worship claim.
The greatness of an oath if they knew does not specify a related claim about worship or divine intent.
It explicitly forbids saying about God what one does not know, the focus's central charge against the speakers' attribution of intent.
It exposes following ancestors without understanding or guidance, closely paralleling the local move from the focus to inherited worship.
It rejects the claim that ancestral practice is sufficient when revelation calls people elsewhere, reinforcing the local ancestral defense.
It condemns assigning partners, sons, and daughters to God without knowledge, directly paralleling the focus's false theological attribution.
It challenges the claim that God could have a child, providing a close corrective to the angel-and-child assertions surrounding the focus.
It states that God could have prevented association, but does not convert that fact into approval of it, directly correcting the focus's inference.
It contrasts revealed limits with people who mislead by desire without knowledge, a related account of unauthorized religious claims.
It records invented allotments for God and associates, an earlier form of assigning religious practice without divine warrant.
It calls self-made prohibitions a loss made foolishly and without knowledge, closely supporting the focus's judgment on fabricated divine intent.
It challenges anyone who attributes a command to God without knowledge, directly matching the focus's evidentiary objection.
People excuse an indecent practice by saying that God commanded it; the verse rejects speaking about God without knowledge.
It expressly prohibits saying about God what one does not know, providing the focus's general epistemic rule.
It says conjecture cannot replace truth, directly reinforcing the focus's conclusion that their claim is only guesswork.
It challenges people who label provision lawful or forbidden without God's permission, a direct parallel to inventing divine authorization.
It rebukes the claim that God has taken a child as speech made without knowledge, closely matching the surrounding angel claim.
It condemns attributing to God what people themselves dislike and speaking falsely about the outcome, extending the gendered inconsistency near the focus.
It forbids declaring things lawful or forbidden by one's tongue and thereby inventing a lie about God, a direct parallel in unauthorized attribution.
It denies that God has taken a child or has a god beside Him, supplying a close theological correction to the focus's setting.
It identifies the claim that God has begotten as part of the speakers' falsehood, directly continuing the critique of their angel assertions.
It again challenges the claim that God chose daughters over sons, a direct counterpart to the focus's gendered attribution.
It records worshippers defending intermediaries as a means of nearness to God, a related attempt to justify worship by an alleged divine arrangement.
It asks whether associates have authorized a religion God never permitted, directly countering the focus's claim that divine will authorized worship.
It demands a prior book as evidence for the local claim, immediately exposing the absence of warrant behind the focus's assertion.
It restates the defense of inherited religion in the same local argument, showing how unsupported worship is sustained through ancestral precedent.
It challenges the unequal allocation of males to the speakers and females to God, directly mirroring the premise behind the focus's angel claim.
It calls that allocation an unjust division, supplying the evaluative judgment on the gendered claim surrounding the focus.
It says their named objects have no authority and that they follow only conjecture and desire, directly matching the focus's worship and guesswork logic.
It condemns naming angels with female names, the closest parallel to the local assertion about the angels in 43:19-20.
